21003:
Hi Adam,

If you want to treat the MAME debugger as a sort of virtual tape drive for AstroBasic programs, it will probably work better if you load and save the portion of memory from !4000 to !4E7B.  That way, you save the screen contents, the Basic and array program space, the TXTUNF end of basic pointer, and the values of the one and two letter variables, without clobbering any of the interpreter's working space.  I know that a standard AstroBasic :INPUT command saves from !4000 to !4E91 including the checksum byte, but saving and loading the area from !4000 to !4E7B in the debugger has worked for me.

On January 30, 2024, Tony Mokonen wrote, "If you want to treat the MAME debugger as a sort of virtual tape drive for AstroBasic programs, it will probably work better if you load and save the portion of memory from !4000 to !4E7B."

Thanks for the advice, Tony.  I will look into these recommendations.  Ken Lill told me privately that the 4KB file of the AstroBASIC program "Tunneller," that I dumped using the MAME debugger yesterday and posted in this thread, doesn't contain the BASIC program; it only contains part of it.  I asked him to elaborate here in this thread.  Until that happens, I'm holding off on continuing to work on this subject.  I expect that Ken will post here when he has the time.

And yet... I did dig a little deeper in BASICarts and found some more information that might help Ken.  Let's go!

Although I have used BASICarts many times, I haven't investigated the creation of BASICarts too deeply-- yet these BASIC programs have always intrigued me.  In the Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ, here:

https://ballyalley.com/faqs/astrocade_cart_and_hardware_faq.txt

Mike White, who made most (nearly all?) of the BASICarts is quoted in the FAQ about BASICarts:

----------

BASICarts
     Self-Published                            8K cart  1986.
This title encompasses MANY games and other Astrocade software that were
originally tape releases, but are now available as cartridges. Any BASIC game
can be made into a BASICart, and many were. Here's a summary of the situation
from Michael White, the man behind this service: "As early as 1978 Bally sales
hyped the Basic 6002 saying "with this you can write your own game", but
experts claimed it was impossible to run BASIC from the cartridge slot. In
1985, while visiting John Perkins, Leroy Flamm learned of a third start in BRB
through a user vector at 6DD2H. Leroy had an idea for putting Blue RAM Utility
(which is partially written in BASIC), into a game cartridge! Leroy's scheme
was pure genius! When it failed to start he solicited help from two skeptics,
Don Gladden and myself. I got it working with a call to 2164H. Next came
AstroBASIC, and the disbelieving software producers were informed in March 1986
that cassette games could be put on cartridges, but there was NO ONE interested
in selling BASICarts! So ads were made and the whole thing went public,
beginning with an ad in August 1986. Believe it or not!"  Designed by Mike
White. (Arcadian vol.7 pg.57,59,87,90)

----------

Mike White wrote a series of Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC tutorials called "Tricks of the Trade" which can be read on BallyAlley.com, here:

https://ballyalley.com/basic/tutorials/tutorials.html

Somewhat to my own amazement, I haven't read all of Mike's tutorials.  Mike's "Tricks of the Trade #19: Beyond Repack" covers, "Repack (Part 2), Multiple Loading (Part 1), File Search (Part 3), Bankswitching and BASICarts."  Creating the BASICart is discussed on pages 4-6.  This tutorial is here:

https://ballyalley.com/basic/tutorials/Beyond_Repack.pdf

I didn't realize (or maybe I've forgotten) that, according to Mike White in this article, Ken Lill coined the term BASICart.

Ken, please take a look at this tutorial and report back in this thread if this is the missing information and Z80 machine language listing that you're seeking to create new BASICarts.

21019:
MCM Design Hi-Res News - Report 6, Part 2
Piggy-Backing 2 Composite Video Driver Schemes onto an Astec RF Modulator

Part 2 details the 2 video driver schemes described in Part 1 for use with the existing Astec RF modulator normally used in the Astrocade home computer.

Photos are attached showing the bread boarded piggy-back setups.

LOWERING THE VIDEO LINE 3.3K R33 RESISTANCE WILL INCREASE THE TV DISPLAY'S CLARITY

A long time ago I discovered that replacing the 3.3K R33 resistor on the Astrocade motherboard with a lower resistance will increase the clarity on the TV display.

The R33 resistor, wired in series with the custom data chip's video output line at the chip pin 24, is located near the RF modulator 8 pin connector. This resistor is shown on the motherboard schematic and component layout drawings in the Bally Service Manual PA-1, which is archived on the BallyAlley.com website.

Recently I piggybacked a 3.3K resistor on top of R33 with only 1 resistor lead soldered, so I could push down the loose resistor lead onto the other side of R33. When the menu was displayed, there was an obvious increase in clarity when the piggybacked resistor was pushed downward to make contact with R33. Two 3.3K resistors in parallel will yield an effective resistance of 1.5K ohms.

I have asked the question if lowering the series R33 resistor to 1K ohms would increase the custom data chip's video output line current enough to create a situation which might raise the chip's operating temperature hotter than it was designed to operate at.

One could probably use a kitchen digital thermometer having a metal probe to monitor the custom data chip's plastic package temperature. Perhaps the thermometer could sense a temperature increase comparing a 1K resistor installation versus the normal 3.3K factory installation. I haven't actually run any data chip operating temperature test.

For years, I have been running my hi-res Astrocades with a 1K R33 to get that higher TV display clarity. Because I run my Astocades with forced air cooling, there has been no issues. The custom data chip never runs hot to the touch.

I also suspect that both the custom address and the custom data chip will both operate a little hotter in the hi-res mode compared to low-res operation. I wouldn't give my reasons for this claim here in this posting.

You only need a little air passing over the data chip. A 120vac mini fan purchased at Jameco Electronics, set up to blow a little air over the motherboard data chip, would be sufficient.

Users who run their Astrocade with the console top in place should probably not attempt any R33 modification.

THE THS7314 VIDEO DRIVER SCHEME

In Part 1, I indicated this scheme seemed to be just a little clearer than the DataMax UV-1R video driver scheme.

I piggybacked the THS7314 schematic, shown in Part 1, on top of a very old (45 years?) Astec modulator. The attached photos show my set up. The motherboard still had the factory installed 3.3K R33 resistor.

You can use the small LM78L05 regulator (Jameco part #51182?) to lower the modulator input +10v to +5v or tap +5v from the motherboard C67 0.1uf bypass capacitor solder pad. One end of the cap (toward custom data chip) is +5v. The other side is gnded.

The set up was powered on and to my surprise, the video driver wasn't working right. I saw 2 issues. The Seawolf game playing field was terribly filled with some kind of interference. What?

This driver scheme runs great on my final hi-res Astrocade. Then I recalled my hi-res Astrocades use 1K R33 resistors.

The THS7314 scheme utilizes a 1200 ohm resistor wired from the video input line to gnd. This resistor is probably being used as a voltage step down for the THS7314 video input. I thought the 3.3k R33 resistor on this low-res Astrocade motherboard might be creating too low of a voltage swing at the THS7314 video input.

So I replaced the 3.3K R33 with a 1K resistor. When this revision was powered on, I ran some low-res games. My reaction was wow! I ran Checkmate, the Store Demo, Seawolf and the Incredible Wizard. Now this video driver was running as good as the same scheme on my final hi-res Astrocade. What a major improvement compared to the RF modulated display.

At this time, the THS7314 chip is readily available at Mouser Electronics for under $1.
595-THS7314D, $0.94, will ship separately in a mini static proof box?
595-THS7314DR, $0.70, will ship sandwiched between a "sticky tape" and placed in a static proof pouch?

Don't let the tiny size of this chip intimidate you into not choosing to build this high performance, low component count, composite video driver.

Yes, this is a tiny 8 pin SMD, however, you only have to solder pins 1, 4, 5 and 8, which are the SMD package end pins. Pins 2, 3, 6 and 7 are not connected.

For a pro-grade PC board, you would only need to provide solder pads for pins 1, 4, 5 and 8. Otherwise, you can buy a high quality SMD to DIP breakout board at www.schmalztech.com. Choose 8, 14 or 16 pin breakout boards ($1.39 each, must buy qty of 5).

I used a cheap 25W Weller soldering iron with a Weller MT1 tip. Ideally, a long pencil type tip would be a better choice.

For the first pin soldering, I taped down the chip in the desired location using masking tape. I also placed tape over the neighboring pin to help prevent solder spill over. I repeated similarly, to solder the other 3 pins.

I also used an ohmmeter to check neighboring pins for a short due to a miniscule solder spill over.

THE DATAMAX UV-1R VIDEO DRIVER SCHEME

Note that this scheme may also require a 1K R33 resistor for optimum performance.

I found this scheme's performance really close to the THS7314 scheme.

You will have to deal with a few more components and choose transistors that are compatible with a video driver application. I listed some possible transistor choices in Part 1.

Note also that you can NOT plug the transistors directly into a breadboard. Apparently, the underlying breadboard connections will affect the driver's performance, producing false colors. Instead, wire wrap or solder the components on a small hobby board. Then place the hobby board on top of the breadboard. Insert the +5v, -5v, gnd, video in and video out lines into your breadboard. See the attached photo.

THE AUDIO OUTPUT LINE

Add an electrolytic coupling capacitor to the audio line with its positive polarity lead wired toward the custom I/O audio output line pin 24. I used a 47uf 16v electrolytic.

RUNNING A PERFORMANCE TEST

When performance testing your piggyback set up, you might have to (want to) tweak the TV display parameter sharpness, brightness or color intensity to your preference.

IF YOU HAVE THE EXPERTISE
GIVE IT A GO

Tired of seeing a modulated TV display with waves, swirls and snow. Consider bread boarding one of these 2 composite video driver schemes.

Don't forget to replace the 3.3K R33 resistor with a 1.5K or 1k resistor and consider using forced air cooling.

The components for either video driver scheme are cheap.

Cut down a quick-connect breadboard or just mount the longer version to the removable modulator top cover using  number 2-56 screws/nuts.

Use a 3.5mm video out jack instead of RCA phono jacks.

If you are just going to use a 3.5mm male to RCA male stereo audio adapter cable, use an ohmmeter to determine which RCA plug is the video plug and tag it as "Video".

Welcome to the world of composite video. Say goodbye to modulated video.

End of Report 6, Part 2

I worked on some pre-JPEG and pre-MPEG compression technologies.
One of note was Color Cell Compression ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_Cell_Compression). ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_Cell_Compression )

Prior to that, we were looking into bit-dithering techniques, and honestly, I've forgotten most of the work, but at the time we were working on some cutting edge bit dithering algorithms.

Since it has been a while and I don't have access to my old code, I did a search and found this interesting article about bit dithering techniques... (Algorithms and source code)
https://tannerhelland.com/2012/12/28/dithering-eleven-algorithms-source-code.html

The irony is that I was working with computers (like the Mac 128) when I was doing the bit dithering coding. I never thought to go back and code it for the Bally Arcade. Hmm... That would have been fun.

Viewing these pictures was either slow or VERY slow, depending on how you wanted the final IFF picture (the standard image format on the Amiga) to look when the original picture was processed.  Thankfully, any already-preprocessed IFF loaded nearly instantly on the Amiga-- it was the conversion process that took a long time.

I just wish that the Astrocade had more ROM space available than the 8K.  I suppose Chris could choose to support the RAM upgrades such as the Blue Ram, Viper, 64K RAM board, or Lil' White Ram, but those are rare (extremely rare!). The limiting factor is the low-resolution of the Astrocade: 160x102 (the programs output is 160x100, leaving some RAM available to display the program). 21027: When you realize that the Mac 128 had a resolution of 512 x 342 1-bit pixels (B&W) in 1984, the Bally Arcade was doing very well with their 320 x 204 multi-bit color display when it came out in 1977. Almost 7 years before Macintosh!
21028:
On February 7, 2024, Brett Bilbrey said, "When you realize that the Mac 128 had a resolution of 512 x 342 1-bit pixels (B&W) in 1984, the Bally Arcade was doing very well with their 320 x 204 multi-bit color display when it came out in 1977."

Agreed, the Bally Arcade was doing well with its chipset in 1977/1978.  The 4K of RAM did limit the "consumer" version of the Bally custom chipset to 160x102, while the "commercial" version used in the arcades had, at least, 16K of RAM, to use the hi-res 320x204 mode.  Simply adding RAM to the Bally Arcade/Astrocade home console didn't allow it to use the hi-res mode; the console had to be modified, which isn't trivial.  Michael Matte, a member here, does describe this upgrade in his documentation from 1984/1985 and 2019, here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/hi-res_packages/hi-res_packages.html

John Perkins (of Perkins Engineering, the company that sold the Blue Ram and other Bally Arcade console upgrade) also designed a hi-res Astrocade, which you can see here:

https://ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/Hi-Res_Astrocade/Hi-Res_Astrocade.html

Michael Matte does describe his hi-res Astrocade in his videos, here:

https://www.youtube.com/@mcmsastrocades9366/videos

Yes, the Bally custom chipset is incredible for 1977/1978.  However, that power came with a price that was so expensive that it was only used in arcade systems, with "Seawolf II' being the first in 1978.  There was really only one computer made that used the Bally custom chip set in the early 1980s: the ZGRASS/UV-1 computers.  Here is a price list from 1983 for the various versions of the ZGRASS systems:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/datamax-1983_price_list.pdf

This Z-GRASS computer did have MANY upgrades to accomplish its special animating task, including: a 5.5 MB hard drive(!), disk drives, a large RAM drive, a graphics tablet, a special monitor and more, to name only a few of the upgrades).  Still, the price of a fully decked-out ZGRASS system was extremely steep at about $17,000 (seventeen-thousand dollars).  Upon release, the Macintosh 128 retailed for about $2,500 (two-thousand five hundred dollars).  The differences between the original Mac and the ZGRASS computers is great, both in price, performance and usage.  Luckily, one version of the UV-1 (a stripped down ZGRASS unit) also cost about $2,500 and is detailed in the above price list.  It should please Chris Martin that the video digitizer hardware for the Z-GRASS, which isn't included in any of the above prices, cost an additional $2,000.  The "Bally Astrocade Image Works" software does the work of that hardware for free.

It sounds like I don't agree with Brett, but I most certainly do agree with him.  The Astrocade, which sold for $300 in January 1978, and had Bally BASIC released in around September 1978, was a bargain, even with its low-resolution.

Sorry, I'll provide a bit more info. The OSCR, Also called Sanni's Open Source Cart Reader, is an Arduino shield, which dumps to an SD card, and is standalone (aside from flashing updates from PC to the Arduino).
The current hardware revision 5 has built-in slots for Gameboy/Gameboy Advance, NES, SNES, Famicom, Genesis/MegaDrive, Sega Master System, and N64. It also has a connector for N64 controllers to dump their memory cards.
Then many adapters are available to build as software to support more consoles is added. They get pretty niche (Pokemon Mini with only like 10 games released has an adapter).
You can make it yourself, buy a kit, or buy prebuilt ones from people. I do not recommend getting one from Aliexpress though, we see too many issues with those.
There's more info on the github here:GitHub - sanni/cartreader: A shield for the Arduino Mega that can back up video game cartridges.

I'm happy to answer any questions I can. I'm semi involved in the project and helped with minor bugfixes/additions but am no means a dumping script writer.
Here's mine, which has a 3D printed shell (optional) with dust cover. Gameboy slot is on the rear.

I think that information about why "Muncher" potentially wasn't released is still in the current FAQ, but not the general Astrocade FAQ.  It is in the "Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ," here:

https://ballyalley.com/faqs/astrocade_cart_and_hardware_faq.txt

I have quoted the whole section on Pac-Man/Munchie/Let's-Call-It-Whatever-Today, here:

------------------------------

Pac-Man
     Astrocade Inc.                                   8K cart  1985.
AKA No-Die, Pacmen, Munchie.  Astrocade was forbidden to release this game by
a court order (rumors claim that Astrocade spent a fortune in litigation with
Atari, but to no avail!). The prototype, actually titled "Pac Man," turned up
with Clyde Perkins and Phillip Harris in 1983. Phillip changed the title to
Muncher, and sold two batch runs with a white label that reads, "TEST
PROGRAMME" (these were sold through the "Arcadian" newsletter). Then another
unknown source (Esoterica?) sold more "Muncher" cartridges with a red label
that says "DEMO". Esoterica did release an unknown quantity under the red
"MUNCHER" label. Only Mike White sold any (very few) after 1984 as Pacman (the
original Clyde Perkins/prototype version). No-Die is this same program with
infinite lives and the scratchpad made visible as per Dave Carson (Arcadian
vol.6 pg.40). Pacmen is also the same with any number of lives you wish! (See
Arcadian vol.6 pg.48) Michael kept track of the number of cartridges sold,
under various names (each with a different "tweak"), here's the breakdown: Pac
Man (21), No Die (4), Pacmen (1). All of these cartridges ride a very fine line
between prototypes and copies. Other names attributed to this title (but not
distributed on cartridge) are: "Munch Kid", "Munchkin", "Peckmen" and "PacSam".
(Arcadian vol.3 pg.63,121, vol.4 pg.33,55, vol.5 pg.45,77,92,106,135,163, vol.6
pg.1,14,40,48, vol.7 pg.13,46,67,94, Michigan Astrobugs Newsletter May 83 pg.2,
Aug.83 pg.2,5, Nov.83 pg.6,7, MAR.84 pg.1, JUL.84 pg.2, Niagara Bug Bulletin
vol.1 pg. 3,4, vol.)  According to a talk/interview called "From Tron to
Curveball: Bill Adams' Life in Classic Gaming" that Bill Adams gave at the
Southern-Fried Gameroom Expo 2016, the code for Pac-Man for the Bally
Arcade/Astrocade was used as the code-base for the video portion of the
arcade/pinball hybrid game "Baby Pac-Man." (Interview available at:
https://www.brokentoken.com/podcast-episodes/episode-43-next-exit-silicone-
valley/).  Written by Bill Adams.

------------------------------

That's a lot of names for one game!  If I run into any proof as to why there is no official release of "Pac Man" on the Astrocade, then I'll try to remember to post it here.

While looking for the answer to Michael's question about Atari vs. Astrocade, Inc., I searched files that aren't uploaded to BallyAlley.com too. Many of these files are on archive.org.  Here are links to them:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/Archives/Archives.html

Maybe searching through these files will pull up what you're looking for now, Michael.  If not, then have fun going through all of those files; there are thousands of them!

Phillip changed the title toMuncher, and sold two batch runs with a white label that reads, "TESTPROGRAMME" (these were sold through the "Arcadian" newsletter). Then anotherunknown source (Esoterica?) sold more "Muncher" cartridges with a red labelthat says "DEMO". Esoterica did release an unknown quantity under the red"MUNCHER" label. Only Mike White sold any (very few) after 1984 as Pacman (theoriginal Clyde Perkins/prototype version). No-Die is this same program withinfinite lives and the scratchpad made visible as per Dave Carson (Arcadianvol.6 pg.40). Pacmen is also the same with any number of lives you wish! (SeeArcadian vol.6 pg.48) Michael kept track of the number of cartridges sold,under various names (each with a different "tweak"), here's the breakdown: PacMan (21), No Die (4), Pacmen (1). All of these cartridges ride a very fine linebetween prototypes and copies. Other names attributed to this title (but notdistributed on cartridge) are: "Munch Kid", "Munchkin", "Peckmen" and "PacSam".(Arcadian vol.3 pg.63,121, vol.4 pg.33,55, vol.5 pg.45,77,92,106,135,163, vol.6pg.1,14,40,48, vol.7 pg.13,46,67,94, Michigan Astrobugs Newsletter May 83 pg.2,Aug.83 pg.2,5, Nov.83 pg.6,7, MAR.84 pg.1, JUL.84 pg.2, Niagara Bug Bulletinvol.1 pg. 3,4, vol.)  According to a talk/interview called "From Tron toCurveball: Bill Adams' Life in Classic Gaming" that Bill Adams gave at theSouthern-Fried Gameroom Expo 2016, the code for Pac-Man for the BallyArcade/Astrocade was used as the code-base for the video portion of thearcade/pinball hybrid game "Baby Pac-Man." (Interview available at:https://www.brokentoken.com/podcast-episodes/episode-43-next-exit-silicone-valley/).  Written by Bill Adams.

21059:
What I've always assumed (with no concrete proof, mind you) is this: After buying Midway around 1969, Bally put its own name on slot machines, pinball tables, etc. while reserving Midway's name for the arcade video games once they started manufacturing those. That's why you'll only see the name "Midway" (without "Bally") on the title screens of Space Zap, Wizard of Wor, Gorf, Pac-Man, Ms. Pac-Man, Rally-X, Bosconian, etc.

But for whatever reason, Bally made itself, not Midway, the so-called consumer division, so the name "Bally" appeared on the HOME system, that of course being the Professional Arcade.

At some point in 1981, Bally consolidated, or at least cleaned up a few things. First of all, the joint name "Bally/Midway" began to appear on arcade marquees and title screens, beginning (I think) with the Adventures of Robby Roto. Secondly, the Professional Arcade was sold to Astrovision, which, as Michael has indicated, subsequently changed its name to Astrocade. The reason was that Astrovision, as I read in an issue of Electronic Games from that period, was found to be an already existent manufacturer of pornographic video tapes.

Under the terms of the sale, Astrocade was allowed to label its console the "Bally Astrocade" for one year, but it didn't have the rights to the arcade titles -- those weren't part of the deal. A couple of games' titles were therefore changed. Voila! Mystery solved......IF this is true.

Now, presumably, Astrocade could have paid Bally to license the cartridge rights to the games that hadn't already been scooped up by Atari (including Pac-Man), but chose not to, instead renaming Space Zap to Space Fortress. That's actually the only non-Atari-obtained arcade conversion for the Astrocade that I can think of.

I might have a detail or two wrong, but I trust someone will set me straight if that's the case!

Last night I played WaveMakers' "Monkey Jump/Gong the Kong" for about 40 minutes.  Is anyone interested in playing this game and exploring it with me?  Even if you don't have a real Bally Arcade/Astrocade console, then you can still play it.  Both of these AstroBASIC games (really, it is one game with the different levels being its own "game") work fine in MAME.  I even used an Astrocade hand controller, but you'll need the Astro-dapter to be able to use one under emulation.  You can choose to play the game with any controller you have handy, or just the arrow/cursor keys.

Here are a couple of observations about "Monkey Jump/Gong the Kong:

1) This game is NOT easy.

2) This game's character movement is semi-annoying, but it's written in BASIC, so I give it a pass.  Also, you get used to the way the character moves and learn to work within those limitations.

3) The game's graphics are "blinky" and primitive-- just like all games written in Bally BASIC/Astrocade.

I did post links to the game and information about it already in the "Bally vs Atari" thread, here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/message/21061

Astrocade fans, I would love to have an excuse to play this game.  I don't want to play it alone, come and join me and let's play it together and post about our gameplay experiences here.

On February 17, 2024, Allen Schweitzer wrote, "I have 'Monkey Jump/Kong the Kong' on cassette, but I've never loaded a game onto a console before."

First: avoid loading any game or program from a real tape or cassette.  These Astrocade tapes are 40 years old or older.  The best of them won't load for me without trouble now.  Even back in the 1980s, Astrocade users had difficulties loading software from tape.  What to do?  Load software that has been digitally archived.  If you have one-of-a-kind software that has not been digitally archived yet... then archive it first (and post it here so that it can be added to BallyAlley.com or archive.org).

Loading a digitally archived game onto the Astrocade with AstroBASIC is easy.  Also, now that MAME supports loading Astrocade software from "tapes" (WAV files), that is probably even easier to do for many people.  However, Allen, since you repair Astrocade consoles, you need to experience loading software onto the real hardware.  It only takes about 20 seconds to load any AstroBASIC program that doesn't require expansion RAM (which is literally 99% of the AstroBASIC program library; many hundreds of programs).  If you're going to avoid real hardware (which is how many people must use Astrocade software now), then my video called "Loading and Saving Astrocade AstroBASIC Tapes using MAME Emulation" will get you started:

Replace C63 and C64 capacitors, if I'm not mistaken.  I wouldn't be surprised if it completely comes back to life after you replace C7, C8 and C62-64, just because they are the KEMET caps.  Those things are complete junk and will cause all sorts of problems they shouldn't.

I have OCRed, proofread and corrected the instructions for "Monkey Jump/Kong the Kong" by WaveMakers.

Here is the documentation for WaveMakers Tape 13:

----------------------------------------

NOW the number 1 coin-op game DONKEY KONG is simulated in Astro-BASIC and it's called:

MONKEY JUMP

For 1 to 4 Players

WaveMakers MONKEY JUMP
By MIKE PEACE (C) 1982
TAPE 13

MONKEY JUMP is an exciting game of skill for 1 to 4 players.

SIDE 1. All players use their own control handle.
SIDE 2. For all those who have only one or two handles, players use handle #1.

GAME INSTRUCTIONS

STARTING THE GAME

Using hand control #1, turn the knob until the desired number of players appears on the screen. Pull the trigger and play will begin.

PLAYING THE GAME

The hand control functions are:

TRIGGER  - Makes monkey jump and climb ladders
KNOB     - No function
JOYSTICK - Moves monkey in desired direction. Up joystick has no function

OBJECT OF GAME

To collect all the banana chips from each platform of the structure without getting hit by the hunter, falling in holes, or falling off a ladder.

To begin, you control the monkey located on the bottom left of the structure. Each player has his own banana chips to collect and remains at his own level of play. To collect the chips move the monkey next to them and they will be picked up. You must jump over each hole by holding the joystick in the direction you wish to jump and pulling the trigger, jump over the hunter in this way. To climb a ladder, center the monkey on the ladder and pull the trigger. (You cannot climb a ladder that does not touch the platform floor, or does not clear the platform ceiling.)

To come down the ladder, center the monkey just slightly to the left of center and pull back on the joystick. You cannot use a ladder that does not go at least one rung past the floor or does not touch the floor you are going to. (The monkey must be able to touch the sides of the ladder with his hand to go down)

After completing a level you will go to the next, there will be more holes and each one will be slightly larger than the previous level. More care is needed to get across without falling through.

SCORING

Each banana chip is worth 1 x level

Jumping over the hunter is worth 5 x level

At level 8 each chip is worth 9 or 11 points

Level 8 is the most difficult, if you don't make it you start at level 7 again

EXTRA GAME ON THIS TAPE

Enter the 3rd or 4th loading from the tape and play GONG THE KONG.

Following the same hand control functions as MONKEY JUMP, walk over each bolt to remove it and make the structure collapse and you GONG THE KONG. But watch out for the hunter.

----------------------------------------

21115:
I have added a video review of "Monkey Jump" released by WaveMakers in 1982 for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  This AstroBASIC game was released on WaveMakers Tape 13 and was written by Mike Peace.  The second level of the game, which is a separate BASIC game, is called "Gong the Kong."  I also cover it in this video.  I used the MAME Astrocade emulator to play this game and recorded the footage with OBS Studio.  I think the colors are a bit "off," but the game plays fine.

You can watch the 15-minute video here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TxJPDj2mYDg

This is written on the front cover of the tape's insert:

"NOW the number 1 coin-op game DONKEY KONG is simulated in Astro-BASIC and it's called: MONKEY JUMP."

The object of the game is to collect all the banana chips from each platform of the structure without getting hit by the hunter, falling in holes, or falling off a ladder.

After completing a level, you will go to the next, there will be more holes and each one will be slightly larger than the previous level. More care is needed to get across without falling through.  Next play "GONG THE KONG."  Walk over each bolt to remove it and make the structure collapse and you GONG THE KONG. But watch out for the hunter.

The video is split into four main parts:

0:00 - Narration and overview of Bally Artillery
1:07 - Monkey Jump (Gameplay)
5:42   Monkey Jump (BASIC Listing)
7:07 - Gong the Kong (Gameplay)
13:47 - Gong the Kong (BASIC Listing)

I made this video because my buddy Chris has been posting videos to my BallyAlley YouTube channel over the last couple of weeks.  Also, I have participated in a few videos with my friend Brian on his YouTube channel called Ballistik Coffee Boy.  I didn't want to be left out of all of the fun, so I created a video too.  I chose "Monkey Jump" because I hope that someone will see this video and decide to compete with other Astrocade fans for a high score in this thread:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/play_monkey_jump_kong_the/104400772

I'm promoting the videos by Chris and Brian here because they're both awesome.  These two got me to play my Astrocade again after being distracted by the Timex/Sinclair 2068 computer (another system featuring the Z80 CPU).

If Atari interests you, and you wanna see my pretty face, then check out this video called 'That Atari Show 63: "Frantic For ANTIC!" ( w/ Special Guest, Bally Alley), Newsline & Kay Savetz.'  This video's description says, "This time on 'That Atari Show,' special guest ballyalley (Adam) joins us to discuss Antic Magazine, Atari's #1 Resource that ran from 1982-1990. Adam & (me) BCB go over 50+ issues that Adam gifted me! Why am I talking in third person here? Argh. Oh, and a ton of Atari News! From 'Lunar Lander Beyond' to 'Qomp 2' to Atari 400 Games & more! Plus: Creator Space features KaySavetz!"  The full video is here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Uxpyfkx9_RU

Here is a shortcut to about 20 minutes into the video where the "Feature" begins with Brian and me chatting about Atari magazines from the 1980s:

https://youtu.be/Uxpyfkx9_RU?t=1249

I'll highlight Chris's latest video that was posted four days ago, which features "Save Mary!" a game written in about 1990 for the Atari 2600.  Chris describes his video as "This is a film I made for the Classic-Gaming Webcast, a channel I had in 2013. It features the unreleased game Save Mary! and the three cartridges released by Mythicon in 1983 called Fire Fly, Sorcerer and Star Fox. These are all Atari 2600 VCS titles. At the end is the usual recommendation for our website, Orphaned Computers & Game Systems. Thanks as always to Adam for hosting this on his Bally Alley channel."  You can watch the "Save Mary!" video created by Chris here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=orbDUsNRvII

Let's get back to the Astrocade.  Now that I've posted this video for the AstroBASIC version of "Monkey Jump," I hope to make a short video of the RAM-Expansion-required version of the game played using Blue Ram BASIC.  The game is more colorful and it has improved graphics, yet the gameplay remains the same.

Have fun!

21118:
Personally, I would only heat sink the custom data chip.  Be cautious about using a "high finned" heat sink if you have the protective board on your keyboard wires.  This will more likely than not cause the keypad to slide out of the keyboard when it's all put together.  If you just have wires, you should be OK.  It might not hurt to heat sink the I/O chip, but make sure you have a way to identify the 2 if you heat sink them both.  The I/O is not far behind the data chip as far as failure rate.

  The main things that would cause the symptoms you describe are C6, possibly C1 and any custom chip. To do an immediate check on the customs without removing them is to check for excessive heat. The DATA chip will be quite hot but the other ones should be warm at best. to check the capacitors, you'll need to lift the positive lead and see if any of the voltages come back. DO NOT DO THIS FOR ANY LENGTH OF TIME. You we be adding more stress. The positive leads are the ones closest to you when you are putting in a cartridge. make sure that the wire from the diode is going to this side. The next step would be to quickly pass your hand over the components on the board. The large heat sink on the regulator will be hot, as will the heat sink on the 10V regulator. The 15v (or maybe you have the 12V unit) regulator should be relatively cool. I have found even the tiniest of parts can get very hot if they are bad.The best way to check the customs is to remove them all. then if the voltages come up, replace them one at a time. MAKE SURE YOU DON"T GET THEM MIXED UP!!! They have their power pins in different spots. If left on in the wrong socket, it can fry that chip fairly quickly.
If these tests don't get any of the 3 voltages back, there is a serious problem with some component. There is a short somewhere.

On February 27, 2024, Jeff K. wrote, "I am new to the Astrocade system.  I am most familiar with Z-80 based retro computers, which brought me here.  Thanks Adam T, for pointing me to this online group."

I'm glad you're here, Jeff.  Soon you'll find that the Bally Arcade/Astrocade is a good system from1978 with a weird history that is checkered with missteps.  Could Bally or Astrovision, Inc. have done anything differently to change the fate of the system?  Could any of the dozens of companies from the 1970s to the 1980s have made changes that would have allowed them to survive until today.  Possibly.  I could say that about any of the companies that no one has heard of now.  Would one change have made a difference in the life of the Bally Arcade?  Doubtful.

Jeff continues, "I have been reading some of the newsletters on ballyalley.com.  There is so much great information there"

I'm glad to see that you've taken a shine to the newsletters already.  In around 2001 or 2002, I printed all of the "Arcadian" newsletters and bound them into three books.  I still reference them on a regular basis.

Jeff: "I am working on a very simple project, [...] that I am trying to port to 'any' 70s or 80s computer with a cartridge port, redefinable character sets and a built-in joystick port"

The Bally Arcade does have a cartridge port, but to keep it simple, and because the system was originally meant to be turned into a computer that ran the Z-GRASS programming language, only the most minimal of signals are present at the cartridge port.  All of the other signals must be accessed from the 50-pin connector at the back of the console.

The Astrocade does not have a character set.  It is among the first systems that ONLY has a bitmap display, but you can treat it using BASIC or the built in ROM routines as though it does have a character set.

Since the Astrocade, like the Atari 400/800 has four joystick ports.  Will this make your project any easier, harder or just different, Jeff?  I guess you can just treat the console as though it only has two joystick ports.

I know Jeff from the Timex community, so I do know about his project(s) already.  Please, share them here, Jeff.  They're a bit unusual.

Jeff: "I was not familiar with the Astrocade until Adam mentioned its capabilities in a retro computer meeting."

Jeff is referring to the twice-a-month Timex/Sinclair Zoom meetings that I participate in onm a regular basis.  You can read more about them, here:

https://www.timexsinclair.com/usergroup/timex-sinclair-online-user-group/

Jeff: "I would like to run the Astrocade with Bally Basic under emulation so that I can test the 3x5 custom characters"

Using the 3x5 character set with Bally BASIC or AstroBASIC can be made to work, but it would take up much of the 1.8K of memory available.  Other alternatives are using Blue Ram BASIC, which requires extra RAM (VERY rare on real hardware, but it works using emulation) or programming in machine code, which offers up to 8K of ROM storage.

Jeff: "save the machine code in a REM statement or in unused memory.  I think that the BallyAlley website and YouTube have the resources I need to get started."

Yes, there are plenty of resources on BallyAlley to get you started.  Most questions you have can be answered by someone here.  As for "unused" memory-- you will likely find out soon that there isn't much of that available to you for programming on an unexpanded Astrocade.  The Astrocade was never originally intended to have a programming language running on it without adding RAM. The fact that Jay Fenton wrote Bally BASIC in 1978 and that it works on a system that ONLY has screen RAM is amazing.

Jeff: "I will probably ask quite a few questions as I start this journey."

Ask away, Jeff!

Also, don't get too distracted by those other so-called computers like the Timex/Sinclair and Jupiter Ace.  They're just a passing fad.

I finally got around to purchasing the TL866II Plus (3rd generation) universal programmer, more commonly referred to as the T48 programmer.

Some time ago, Allen Schweitzer introduced me to the earlier version. This tool is very useful for testing loose logic chips and so it will become a great diagnostic tool to check desoldered Astrocade motherboard TTL chips for failures.

I'm hoping the T48 may also test the Astrocade DRAM chips and maybe even give me another option to program my EEPROMs.

I chose to purchase the T48 from Jameco instead of a foreign country. Jameco's price now is nearly $70 excluding S/H and tax. You get the USB cable, but no adapters. I live in western Colorado so the shipping time took less than 1 week.

You can also get the 78 page English User Guide at Jameco but this guide is actually for the upgraded T56 programmer. Testing logic chips is in section 9 in the User Guide. The T48 chip orientation is indicated next to its 40 pin ZIF Socket. Note the User Guide chip orientation is for the T56 48 pin ZIF socket. Apparently a T48 User Guide does not exist.

I ran into an issue when I attempted to download the T48 software from www.xgecu.com into my Windows 10 desktop.

There was no actual software download. What I got was a RAR file that could initialize (set up) the software download.

I have never seen that kind of a file and didn't know what to do with it after I found out the Windows 10 OS could not open it properly.

Jameco provided me with nearly zero support for my download issue. They did give me just enough info to point me in the right direction to resolve my issue.

I lucked out and found a great YouTube video that gave me a step-by-step procedure to unlock (extract) the RAR file, which acts like a zipped folder, so I could run as an administrator the execution file that's within the RAR file.

The application (.exe) file within the RAR file downloads/installs the needed software and driver for the T48 programmer. It placed a Xgpro icon right below my Google Chrome icon. Nice!

The YouTube video I used is entitled:
RAR Files - 3 Ways To Open And Extract Using Windows
9:24 by TechFixFlix

I chose to download the 7-Zip Portable software which was detailed beginning at the time 4:17 in the video.

The 7-Zip Portable download is free and available at the PortableApps.com website.

Beware of this website because it will attempt to distract you with multiple advertisements desiring you to download "who knows what?". All these multiple downloads are marked as "Advertisement". Just follow the above video which will point you to the correct download.

This portable download is suppose to be delete able by Windows, that is, you don't need to uninstall it.

Hello all.

I am Thom Cherryhomes, one of the firmware engineers for the #FujiNet project, which aims to put Wi-Fi network adapters onto every single #retrocomputing and #retrogaming console on Earth.

To date, we've done successful bring-ups for the following systems:

* Atari 8-bit
* Coleco Adam
* Atari Lynx
* Commodore (64/128/VIC20/16/Plus4)
* Apple ][
* Apple Macintosh
* RC2014
* TRS-80 Color Computer
* Atari 2600

and more.

For each, a custom board is designed based around an ESP32 microcontroller, which runs the FujiNet networking stack and manages the various virtual peripherals that are available, such as:

* networked disk drive, to load/use software either via local storage or via the network
* virtual printer, which renders to PDF; emulating a wide variety of printers.
* modem, which can integrate with existing comms programs (depends on the target)
* a network adapter, explained below.

The "disk drive" is the most interesting, basically just providing a way to load software via the Internet, and I use "disk" as a loose term, because e.g. the Atari 2600 version loads cartridge ROMs.

While the "network adapter" is most interesting:

It exposes a device that can open network connections (or sockets) conforming to a given protocol, some of the protocols:

* TCP
* UDP
* FTP
* HTTP/S
* SSH
* TNFS
* SMB
* NFS...

Once a connection is opened, it can be read to, and written from, as well as doing other control commands. One example of this, is to send the contents of the open connection to a JSON or XML parser, so that it can be subsequently queried for specific information.

If you couple the wide range of (expanding) protocols, with the fact that the microcontroller is fast enough to handle connections with cryptography (such as SSL/TLS and SSH), and the fact that there are fully functional JSON and XML parsers, this means that FujiNet devices can communicate with contemporary Internet services directly, without needing an intermediary.

Each bring-up integrates with the target system in a unique way:

* Atari 8-bit uses the SIO connector
* Apple II uses the SmartPort connector
* TRS-80 CoCo uses the Serial (DriveWire) connector
* Atari 2600 plugs into the cartridge port
and so on.

For the Astrocade, it would make sense to use the expansion bus connector, which exposes the entire processor bus, connecting to an RP2040 microcontroller, which serves as the bus front end, and communicates to the ESP32. For any hardware/system-level hackers on here, what do you think?

Potential things to do, would be to add integration into an existing BASIC, to make it easy to write networked applications, as well as making libraries for cross-development solutions.

    On Monday, March 11, 2024 at 04:53:18 PM EDT, thom.cherryhomes@gmail.com <thom.cherryhomes@gmail.com> wrote:  
 
 Hello all.

I am Thom Cherryhomes, one of the firmware engineers for the #FujiNet project, which aims to put Wi-Fi network adapters onto every single #retrocomputing and #retrogaming console on Earth.

To date, we've done successful bring-ups for the following systems:

* Atari 8-bit
* Coleco Adam
* Atari Lynx
* Commodore (64/128/VIC20/16/Plus4)
* Apple ][
* Apple Macintosh
* RC2014
* TRS-80 Color Computer
* Atari 2600

and more.

For each, a custom board is designed based around an ESP32 microcontroller, which runs the FujiNet networking stack and manages the various virtual peripherals that are available, such as:

* networked disk drive, to load/use software either via local storage or via the network
* virtual printer, which renders to PDF; emulating a wide variety of printers.
* modem, which can integrate with existing comms programs (depends on the target)
* a network adapter, explained below.

The "disk drive" is the most interesting, basically just providing a way to load software via the Internet, and I use "disk" as a loose term, because e.g. the Atari 2600 version loads cartridge ROMs.

While the "network adapter" is most interesting:

It exposes a device that can open network connections (or sockets) conforming to a given protocol, some of the protocols:

* TCP
* UDP
* FTP
* HTTP/S
* SSH
* TNFS
* SMB
* NFS...

Once a connection is opened, it can be read to, and written from, as well as doing other control commands. One example of this, is to send the contents of the open connection to a JSON or XML parser, so that it can be subsequently queried for specific information. 

If you couple the wide range of (expanding) protocols, with the fact that the microcontroller is fast enough to handle connections with cryptography (such as SSL/TLS and SSH), and the fact that there are fully functional JSON and XML parsers, this means that FujiNet devices can communicate with contemporary Internet services directly, without needing an intermediary.

Each bring-up integrates with the target system in a unique way:

* Atari 8-bit uses the SIO connector
* Apple II uses the SmartPort connector
* TRS-80 CoCo uses the Serial (DriveWire) connector
* Atari 2600 plugs into the cartridge port
and so on.

For the Astrocade, it would make sense to use the expansion bus connector, which exposes the entire processor bus, connecting to an RP2040 microcontroller, which serves as the bus front end, and communicates to the ESP32. For any hardware/system-level hackers on here, what do you think?

Potential things to do, would be to add integration into an existing BASIC, to make it easy to write networked applications, as well as making libraries for cross-development solutions.

Our whole project is public and open source, now and forever. We create reference designs and firmware, that vendors can put together and provide for their respective communities.

Firmware: https://github.com/FujiNetWIFI/fujinet-firmware
Software: https://github.com/FujiNetWIFI/fujinet-apps

and our discord, where the majority of our development occurs, is here:
https://discord.gg/2Ce9guX

This would have the potential to bring something truly new to the table for Astrocade hackers and users, for quite some time.

Thoughts?

21167:
A note about potential implementation:

With the Macintosh and Atari 2600 versions, we have added an RP2040 microcontroller to the design, alongside the ESP32 microcontroller. This microcontroller is most popularly shipped on the Raspberry Pico.

It is very unique, and represents what I hope to be a major advance to making "software defined peripherals" even easier to implement. It does this by adding what is called a programmable I/O block, or PIO. It is a tiny little nano-processor that has a dozen or so instructions that can be arranged to quickly respond to what's happening on I/O pins. PIO runs asynchronously with the RP2040 and can quickly DMA data in and out of the main memory of the RP2040.

PIO is part of a microcontroller that costs less than 50 cents, IN SINGLE QUANTITIES. This drastically changes the landscape of making peripherals for our beloved machines, because we no longer have to immediately resort to complex programmable logic devices (CPLD) or field programmable gate arrays (FPGA) to handle the vagaries of implement complex hardware circuits in domain specific languages such as Verilog. While complex programmable devices still have a place in making new retro peripherals, we can do most of what's needed on a part that is an order of magnitude cheaper.

So, even with an RP2040, and an ESP32 on the same board, connected via e.g. the UART or SPI, this still works out to a bill of materials cost that is cheap enough for vendors to sell FujiNets at $80 to $90 as of 2024. (A note, we don't build them for vendors, we don't ask for anything, the vendors make and sell. We just want these devices to exist, so we design them, write the firmware, do the hardware reference design, and off everyone else can go.)

----

The other part of this, is application development:

I have extensive experience with developing applications on dozens of platforms, in dozens more of languages. I have looked over the existing documentation, and have a good handle on what the system can do, so I will be able to write example programs, once the hardware is working.

I will primarily be doing this in assembler and C, but is there anyone in this community who knows, for example, how to extend Blue Ram BASIC to add additional commands?

-Thom

Ken Lill on this group probably knows the most about this BASIC variant for an Astrocade with added RAM. The language was disassembled to a great extent by a person named Richard Degler, but he never finished it (or it is finished, but rough). I believe I have that disassembly on my computer-- though I haven't looked at it in a long time. Richard asked me not to share it. The complex part is that the community could use it.  Richard died a number of years ago now and I feel like I'm left with an ethical dilemma: to share or not to share?

For clarity:

Blue Ram BASIC (1980-ish) is an extension of...
Bally BASIC (1978).  BRB was made BEFORE the updated Bally BASIC that is called...
"AstroBASIC" (1981; the BASIC with the built-in tape interface).

"AstroBASIC" is BY FAR the most common BASIC used with the Astrocade because it doesn't require extra RAM or an external tape interface, but Blue Ram BASIC supports extra features, such as more colors available on-screen at one time and more features that escape my memory right now.  Blue Ram BASIC can use the Bally BASIC 300-baud external tape interface to load/save to tape (slow) or the Blue Ram tape interface built into the Blue Ram hardware to save and load at 2000-BAUD.

21171:
On March 13, 2024, Adam Trionfo wrote, "I'll take a look around for the BRB source code/disassembly.  Give me a day or two."

It didn't take me long to find the Blue Ram BASIC disassembly.  It was done between 10-15 years ago!  Like I said, it isn't 100% complete, but it's further along than Richard gave it credit for when he sent these files to Ken Lill and me.  I had forgotten that Richard had also started to disassemble earlier versions of Blue Ram BASIC and Hot Rod Bally BASIC (which later turned into Blue Ram BASIC and ViperSoft BASIC, I think).  There is also a partial disassembly of ViperSoft BASIC, the BASIC version that shipped with the Viper 1 expansion unit and that works with the Lil' White Ram.

Richard was usually disappointed with the feedback that his posted disassembles to the Astrocade group received.  Except from me, there was usually silence.  It wasn't that people didn't care, but most people don't program in Z80.  Therefore, there wasn't much for people so say.  I'm glad to share these files now, when someone may be able to use them as a springboard to help create a new piece of hardware for the Astrocade.

All of the files listed below are in a zip file that I have attached to this post.  I may also place these files on BallyAlley.com, but for now this is the easiest way to share them.

Here are the filenames:

Blue RAM BASIC 1-0 first draft.asm
Blue RAM BASIC 1-1 first draft.asm
BRBASIC 1.0 tape [Not Playable].asm
Hot Rod Bally BASIC first draft.asm
VIPERsoft BASIC (1981) first draft.asm
VSBASIC proto first draft.asm
VSBASIC TAPE first draft.asm

and this one (which may be near completion):

Blue RAM BASICs (Perkins Engineering).asm

It has been a decade since I've looked at these files.  To help me remember what is in the files, years ago, I saved a couple of emails that Richard included with the above files.  These are called:

Blue Ram BASICs Conditional Assembly (2014 07 27)(Richard Degler)[Email_00].doc
Extended BASICs First Draft (2014 07 24)(Richard Degler)[Email_00].doc

I hope that these Z80 source files help out Thomas and others, like Ken Lill who also asked me about Richard's work semi-recently.  There may be questions about these files and the differences between the various versions of BASIC for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade.  Ask the questions and I'll try to jog this wilting memory of mine to answer questions.  Others here can help too.

Thom, let us know what else we can do for you.

21173:
Last night, a friend of mine named Carl was here.  He asked me about how many Astrocades were sold.  He inquired, "Less than a thousand, I guess."  When I told him that probably about 300,000 Astrocades were sold, he didn't believe me.  This is because he is a classic computer fan and collector, and he had never heard of the Bally Arcade/Astrocade until he met me.  He said that the only good thing about it is that it has a Z80 in it (I THINK he was joking).  He said that he would never buy one.  I told him that was okay because increased demand would jack up the price.

I've always known that there is no solid evidence that 300,000 Bally Arcades/Astrocades were sold. I can't even remember where I first encountered this number in the first place.  You can search for this number on the Astrocade discussion group and find some previous talk about it, here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/search?p=recentpostdate%2Fsticky%2C%2C%2C20%2C2%2C0%2C0&q=300%2C000

The most interesting post is one that says the August 1983 of the AstroBUG newsletter mentions that 120,000 Bally Professional Arcade units had been sold at that time.  You can read about that in Kevin Bunch's post here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/message/17606

(In his original post, Kevin says that this number is in the September 1983 issue, but he corrects himself in a later post.)

I could not find this specific newsletter on BallyAlley.com, here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/astrobugs/astrobugs.html

Maybe Kevin meant another newsletter?  Or maybe that issue isn't archived on BallyAlley.com.

"The Bally Astrocade Hardware Guide: Plans, Prototypes and Production [...]" by Michael White, also makes claims to this 120,000 units sold number.  The document is here:

https://ballyalley.com/faqs/bally_astrocade_hardware_guide_faq.txt

It says, "120,000 Arcades had been sold by August of 1983 (9), but the first hint of the system's imminent demise can actually be detected on p. 8 of Arcadian Vol. 1 (12/4/78).  Discontinued in 1984 (10), it's still interesting, fun, and -- to some -- quite a pleasant surprise!"

The footnotes for 9. simply lists, "AstroBugs, p. 4."  I ask, page 4 of which issue?

In the June 1983 issue of "Video Games" magazine, I did find this 120K number in a sentence on page 50 of the article called, "Astrocade: One More Time" by Mark Brownstein:

"The Bally unit, on the other hand, has sold, perhaps, 120,000 units, has had limited television advertising (a short campaign last year under its new name and ownership, Astrocade), until recently no third-party software developers, and remains one of the better-kept secrets in the history of home video game systems."

The article is on BallyAlley.com, here:

https://ballyalley.com/articles_and_news/Astrocade%20-%20One%20More%20Time%20(video%20games)(june%201983)(300dpi)(color).pdf

If you want to lose a few hours of your life, then you will find the complete June 1983 issue of "Video Games" can be read online, here:

https://archive.org/details/video-games-volume-1-number-9-june-1983

I want to definitively know how many Astrocade consoles were sold over its entire lifespan.  Let us keep digging.

The thread named "Serial Numbers," which contains the above post talks about this subject a bit too, here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/78481980

The thread called "Added "Bally Vs. JS&A" Court Document to BallyAlley.com" says that only 3,000 (three thousand, NOT 300,000) Bally Arcade consoles were sold by JS&A, here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/message/10541

I want a solid number written down someplace so that I can point my friend Carl to it.  I don't want to say, "I told you so!"  Well, yeah, I do kinda do wanna tell 'em, "I told ya so!"

Is there a way for us to identify, for certain, how many Astrocade consoles were sold over its entire lifespan from 1978 to 1984?

On March 14, 2024, Thom Cherryhomes wrote, "I connected with Allen Schweitzer, and I'll buy the AV modded Astrocade from him."

It's great news that you'll have an Astrocade, Thom!  Have fun with it.

Thom, you seem to be (very much) a hardware guy.  However, try some of those games.  For a game system designed in 1976/1977 and released and shipped in January 1978, the Bally Arcade can play excellent games.  Try "The Incredible Wizard," the "Wizard of Wor" clone, with two players.  There are many others too.  I think that the Astrocade is the first game console with color, bitmap graphics.  Is there an earlier one?

Thom, since you're a programmer, you might be interested in the "Machine Language Manager" 2K cartridge, a Z80 ML monitor that works in just 2K of RAM.  I have a four-video playlist about it, here:

https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLADcQ67H2uU1dhUPra25rJ3zcfSXMdiKx

Thom continues, "Is there a cartridge PCB and case so that I can quickly make a ZIF socket cartridge for bootstrapping work?"

Ken Lill used to sell bare PCBs that you can then solder on a ZIF socket and use with any 8K EPROM.  Ask Allen if he has any now.  Maybe Ken can make his multicart PCB layout public now?  There are other options too, but probably nothing available to you, Thom.  For instance, the Blue Ram hardware can load a file from tape (nowadays, a WAV file), then you can flip a switch on the unit and it will load as a cartridge from the ROM area. This was the common method to program a cartridge in the 1980s.  Ken, does the Lil' White Ram hardware support this method?

I should have mentioned Rachel Weil's (aka "hxlnt") GitHub site earlier.  She has annotated Z80 assembly source code, binaries, and dev tools for the Bally Astrocade, here:

https://github.com/hxlnt/astrocade

She also made a modern 512K cartridge in 2018 to program an Astrocade called the AstroCart.  You can read about it on AtariAge, here:

https://forums.atariage.com/topic/278401-astrocart-magical-reflashable-512kb-homebrew-cart/

Maybe you can contact her and get one of these cartridges made for yourself, Thom.

You can learn more about Rachel's Astrocade work in this thread, called "About Rachel Weil ("hxlnt") with Links to Videos, Articles, Software Development Tools," here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/103670572

Thom: "Adam, were you able to get clarification from your friend on the Atari FujiNet and its capabilities?"

Yes, I think I had my Atari FuniNet questions answered by my friend a couple of nights ago.  I'm going to order the FujiNet 1.3.

To support both the low and high resolution modes via the 50 pin expansion, you would have to relocate the 40 pin custom address and data chips to the expansion PC board.

The expansion PC board would also require:
a microcycler
four 4KB banks of screen RAM because of the way the hi-res screen RAM is scanned for the TV display.
screen RAM control lines scheme
the hi-res TV display scanning scheme.

The 50 pin expansion bus does not support the required negated 7M clock.
It does support a Video In line (pin number 3) to the RF modulator.

Reference:
Bally Service Manual PA-1 for the Astrocade motherboard schematic.
Nutting Manual low/hi-res system description.

The drawings (archived on the Bally Alley) labeled DWG 2 thru DWG 6 for MCM Design's low/hi-res static screen RAM scheme are obsolete. The revised scheme drawings have NOT been submitted to Adam Trionfo.

My personal observation among the Astrocade users, relating to the possibility of the Astrocade running also in the high resolution mode, is that it is merely an interest of curiosity.

Mister HR (Hi-Res)
of MCM Design

The Network Adapter has a concept of protocol adapters. These do all the
heavy lifting, so that all the Astrocade has to do, is open an I/O channel,
and read/write to it, and send control commands.

One of the protocol adapters is HTTP. It supports HTTPS. This means
SSL/TLS. There are also JSON and XML parsers on the FujiNet. These can
parse complex documents using the FujiNet's considerable internal memory,
and the Astrocade can query for bits and pieces of information that it
wants. This is how programs like weather and ISS are implemented.

To further elaborate the point:

The FujiNet game lobby is a web service. It talks JSON.

The FujiNet can connect to the lobby. It pulls down a list of running game
rooms, and displays them.

User can select from one of those games, and the lobby program again
queries to ask what to mount to load the game, then it loads the game.

More information on the Lobby service here:
http://fujinet.online:8080/ (doc link at bottom of page)

e.g. 5 card Stud

5 Card Stud has its own web service. It talks JSON.

5 card stud client on the Astrocade (or whatever system is using fujinet)
connects to the web service and uses it to ferry game state back and forth.

All of a sudden, multi-user games that cross computer and console become
possible.

More examples of the N: device, from the Atari's perspective.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vqz_AZgxaVY

This opens up a whole bunch of potential applications....

This message is written primarily with Thom Cherryhomes in mind, although it isn't meant to be only read by him (otherwise I would have sent it privately as an email message).

I'm not posting this to the on-going FujiNet thread that began on March 11, 2024, as this is possibly a one-off note, although I'd like to see some others join in too.  If a thread gets started, then I hope it is focused on people, Astrocade owners and users, and not on Astrocade or Astrocade-related hardware.

This Astrocade group isn't always active, and sometimes it takes a bit of prodding to get feedback. The feedback may take a bit of time to come.  I've found that asking general, open-ended questions will get some members to talk.  This is why I asked in a post earlier today about ideas from smart people for Astrocade games that might use the FujiNet.  I hoped, I still hope, actually, that it will bring others forward to put their networked-games ideas, zany and unrealistic, or perfectly realistic, to the group.

In general, since the Astrocade is primarily a game console, most of the members are gamers.  Those with the most tech knowledge are generally older.  For instance, Ken Lill was in his early-30s in the 1980s.  At 51, am I one of the younger members here?  I find that many game collectors and game players make up this group.  Programmers?  Not as much.

There are only two homebrew cartridges on the Astrocade console.  By this, I mean modern games.  If you count some of the older titles, such as those from the early 1980s as "homebrews," then there are several more.

There are not many people who program on the Astrocade for two reasons.  One, the hardware is hard to acquire.  Two, the MAME emulation is just adequate enough to play current games.  This is fine for me and most others, but not for those looking to push the hardware to its limits.  For them, it's a restriction.

As an example, about four years ago, there was a Euro-style demo made for the Astrocade called "Astrocademo."  You can view it here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ksY7Fm8kS68
[cid:dad07d03-93ca-4dd0-9e11-aad5c208044e]<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ksY7Fm8kS68>

In order to get the demo working, the programmers, who didn't have a real Astrocade, had to bounce the program back and forth to me.  This worked fine, but it was a bit time-consuming.  After this demo was finished, the plan was to try to force the hardware to produce hi-res-like graphics, if I understood correctly, by programming it like the Atari 2600.  This might work, but MAME isn't accurate enough for the Astrocade emulation to allow cycle-counting.  At least it wasn't at the time; maybe it is now?

My tech level, both hardware and software-wise, is pretty light.  Also, I have epilepsy.  Lately, I've been having a couple of seizures a week.  This acts kind of as a soft-reset on my brain and it affects my memory.  If I can't keep up with a thread, then you can bet that my brain got scrambled to some extent in the last 24-48 hours.  Yet, I try to still hang in there and participate in the group 'cause, ya know, it's fun!

Thom, if you're searching for some information about the Bally Arcade, then ask on the group and I'll see if I can find it for you.  I also can probably, at least, track down someone who can help you if I can't find what is needed.

Thanks, Thom, for joining the Astrocade group and bringing some new technology to us all.  You just might bring our little console (no, it's a computer!) into the 21st century, even if I'm going along the whole while, kicking and screaming, with my mouth wide open in wonder, uttering, "Now, uh... what do you mean?  What's all this about networking... huh?"

21223:
The custom address and data chip combo is designed to attempt a map to the TV display in the low or high-res mode defined by bit 0 of output port 08H. When bit 0 = 0, the map attempt is in low-res. When bit 0 = 1, the map attempt is in hi-res. Of course, there must be screen RAM hardware to support either map attempt.

MCM Design's static screen RAM scheme includes an automatic low/hi-res screen RAM select scheme that monitors bit 0 of port 8 to support either graphic mode.

So, a single software program can mix the 2 graphic modes, if desired, by simply outputting 00 or 01H to port 8. The program must also set up the usual 4 screen RAM parameters.

The MAME low-res Astrocade emulation does support the hi-res mode partially, that is, it will only map out a top portion of the entire hi-res screen map.

I've heard of blitter graphic hardware, but don't know what graphic capabilities it has. The pattern transfer board (PTB) scheme in the WOW coin-op game acts like a digital machine language (ML) graphics subroutine. The PTB is faster because there are no delays to fetch ML instructions from memory to be executed by the Z80 CPU.

Up to now, I didn't think there really was any Astrocade user interest in a hi-res Astrocade other than curiosity.

I'm now wondering why there seems to be a desire to promote "The Ultimate Astrocade" video. I like the idea, but I don't get the intention behind it.

I have no plans to sell any low/hi-res upgrade kit or fully assembled hi-res Astrocade.

Some time ago I gave notice relating to the features of my final hi-res Astrocade and I also attempted to survey the discussion group which included a possible hi-res Astrocade availability plan. There was no response to these 2 postings. Again, I don't understand why this latest hi-res video seems to be stirring up some possible interest in a hi-res Astrocade.

MCM

That is essentially what the Blitter in the Amiga and later Atari STe computers did.

It moves images from ram to screen and applies various effects like pixel shift, or, xor flip, flop, rotate, etc. The CPU tells the Blitter where and how and the Blitter does the rest.

21236:
Right, the idea of an FPGA is that you can program it to imitate the circuits behind whatever platform (the Bally Arcade, an Atari 7800, whatever) physically on a chip. For the Mister's case that would be the De-10 Nano.
The Mister's hardware design is pretty standardized but fairly simple - at the baseline you need the De-10 Nano, an input/output board, and a USB hub. Pretty sure the Stelladapter works with it to use original BPA controllers, though I've never had the patience to figure out how to make paddle controls work well in general on the thing. There's also an optional audio jack for loading audio files, which at present does nothing on the BPA core because its original author didn't know the system could run cassettes (or had RAM expansions, or could have a keyboard hooked up to it, and so on). In lieu of the keypad, you can either set it up to have the keypad buttons on a keyboard ala mame or map them to a controller. Misteraddons sells pre-built units, though you can save a fair bit of money if you're willing to buy the components yourself and assemble it - even moreso if you know someone who can get a student discount on a De-10, as commercially speaking education is what the company is pushing it for. 

In theory it'd be a great way to play the console, if anyone ever goes back in and implements the missing aspects of the hardware. When I mentioned it to the person who wrote it originally, she remarked it all sounded fairly straightforward but was too focused on other projects to go back to it (and no one else has bothered since then, though I and a couple others have brought it up multiple times as a potential project). I get the distinct impression that the home console's implementation was mostly because the arcade hardware behind GORF and Wizard of Wor is also implemented and they share a lot of internals. 

It's a very handy piece of kit, though. The cores that are well implemented are functionally indistinguishable from the original hardware, and it's worked with pretty much any usb-based controller option or adapter I've thrown at it, with the exception of the Egret II Mini spinner controller (which even MAME has problems with due to how weirdly they coded the device). There's pretty much always something being updated or added to the device, and in that regard it reminds me a lot of MAME's development like 20 years ago.

21241:
If your aim is analog out to a VGA monitor, you're probably going to be out of luck. Since this is using the chip to copy the circuitry of the hardware, that includes the output. Since a VGA monitor doesn't have the same resolution as a regular TV it's going to have problems running the BPA or the Spectrum (which will be looking for NTSC and PAL output). The HDMI out ameliorates this problem since the signal is going through a digital upscale and normalization process. So if that's your use case you're probably better off with software emulation.

You stated that the Amiga and Atari STe computers had a blitter and that a blitter  "moves images from ram to screen and applies various effects like pixel shift, or, xor, flip, flop, rotate, etc".

Based on your definition above, the Bally custom Address/Data chips must have some kind of a built-in blitter which is supported by ROM graphic subroutines. The Nutting Manual uses the terminology Magic RAM and Magic Functions plop, or, xor, flop, expand and rotate.

Unfortunately, I only have a vague listing of the pattern transfer board (PTB) graphic options. I'll likely have to study chip data sheets and run simple ML graphic tests to fully understand how the PTB manipulates graphic patterns.

I'm hoping the PTB can process graphic patterns also from ROM when writing patterns to screen RAM.

I'm also wondering if the PTB can write a pattern to Magic RAM. The Magic RAM and Magic functions processing time might not be able to keep up with the faster PTB processing speed.

With a simple change in the PTB scheme, that is, the hi-res bytes per graphic line (50H) versus the low-res bytes per graphic line (28H), the PTB might be usable in low-res. That will be a possible option worth exploring.

Adam
To answer your question relating to how many Midway coin-ops used the PTB, it looks like the PTB was utilized on Midway's WOW, Gorf and Space Zap coin-ops.

Reference
Midway's Card Rack System Part I
which is a detailed manual viewable as a PDF file.

You asked the question, can the low or hi-res modes be mixed on the same screen?

Not on my hi-res Astrocades. The low and hi-res TV displays do take up the same area on a TV/monitor.

However, you can simulate the low-res mode on a hi-res screen map.

In several of my YouTube videos, I ran the low-res menu/onboard games on my hi-res TV display. The low-res graphics looked "sliced up". That's because low-res maps 40 screen RAM bytes per horizontal line and hi-res maps 80 bytes per line.

In hi-res, the top 1/4 of the screen RAM area maps the RAM addresses 4000 - 4FFFH, so every other low-res graphic pattern line will be written on the left half or the right half of that 1/4 top. The low-res graphics will look sliced up with part of it displayed on the left half and part of it on the right half. Does that make sense?

But wait! There's more.

Remember Perkins modified for hi-res Bally motherboard?

Some time ago, I redrew the only schematic that documents the Perkins hi-res scheme, so the scheme was easier to read for me. I spent a good amount of time studying that drawing attempting to understand what Perkins did with his hi-res vision.

The  Perkins motherboard has the four 2K ROM layout.

It looks like he replaced the U4 ROM with a 4KB EPROM and disabled the U2 ROM so he could alter some ROM locations within the ROM addresses 0000 - 0FFFH. The UPI and all the on board subroutines are in the range 0000 - 0E14H.

Perkins must have copied the low-res UPI/subs and then tweaked the graphic subroutines changing the single byte 28H (40 bytes/line) parameter to 50H (80 bytes/line). Doing that would then display the low-res menu correctly in the upper left quadrant of the hi-res TV display. He raised up the vertical blanking line so it would hide the Z80 stack, variables, flags, etc. Pretty clever.

He also used bit 1 in the output port 08H to enable the medium-res mode.

If Perkins did copy all of the on board subs into the 4KB EPROM, he wouldn't have had a lot of available bytes left to program an awesome medium-res or hi-res demo. Perhaps he removed the Scribbling Menu linked list so he would have a few more extra bytes to create a simple medium-res or hi-res demo as part of the Menu listing.

So it is possible to simulate the low-res mode on a hi-res screen map.

Note to Ken Lill
Ken. If you are reading this post and you still have a failed Perkins modified for hi-res motherboard, I'd like to make time to see if I can troubleshoot and fix that board. I have the expertise, diagnostic tools, including hi-res diagnostics, plus the gift of perseverance to possibly get that bit of Astrocade history up and running. It would be exciting to me and a honor to work on an extremely rare classic piece of video gaming hardware.

Maybe we can work out some kind of trade agreement related to hi-res. If you're interested, let's have an email or phone chat.

It will definitely be time-consuming to breadboard, test and wire wrap the scheme. I will likely save this challenge as the last feature to install.

At this time, March 2024, the upper assembly, which will rest on top of the add-under console, is nearly finished.

The upper assembly will include:
modified for hi-res Astrocade
composite video and audio drivers quick- connect board
low/hi-res screen static RAM (SRAM) Board 1
stars/sparkle colors (SSC) board

The SSC scheme, a slight variation of the SSC scheme documented in the WOW Operating Manual, was bread boarded and mounted on the screen SRAM board 1. The SSC scheme was tested working good.

I had to use the 2 transistor configuration DataMax UV-1R composite video driver (CVD) instead of the THS7314 CVD because it was compatible with the SSC scheme.

The SSC scheme was originally intended to be the featured custom graphics board for "The Ultimate Astrocade" infomercial video.

For example, in the intro title page, a twinkling starfield would be present across the entire TV screen, not just the screen RAM area. Also, the character string "Ultimate" would sparkle.

Unfortunately, the Elgato video capture did not process the SSC graphic option to my satisfaction, so I recorded the video using my original (redesigned) hi-res Astrocade, which was posted as the "MCM Design Hi-Res News - Report 8", May 30, 2023, message #20143. This hi-res Astrocade has no SSC scheme.

This is why all the graphic pages in the hi-res infomercial, except the 13 color page, have a black background. The video was originally intended to show off the SSC graphic option.

Unfortunately I can't to my satisfaction capture as a YouTube video using my Canon camera or using the Elgato what I see on my Toshiba 20"CRT TV when my final hi-res Astrocade is executing "The Ultimate Astrocade" with the SSC board operating. I wish you guys could see that. It is so cool.

The SSC scheme will be wire wrapped and mounted on the screen SRAM board 1 at a later time.

The next step for my final hi-res Astrocade project will be to wire wrap the software selectable low/hi-res graphic mode scheme and all the User RAM/ROM schemes onto Board 2, which will be the top board on the 3 tier horizontal rack inside the add-under console. Since the majority of these schemes have already been tested, I'm not expecting any operating issues.

I'm not sure how the Z-GRASS/add-under hardware would have worked (or, does work, since it exists but was never released).  Although I have the complete (or maybe near-complete) documentation for the Z-GRASS language on my site, I think it is a mix of UV-1/add-under documentation.  I've never really dived into it closely.  It is all here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/zgrass.html

Thom continues, "Seeing that the Astrocade's graphic chip and bus glue lock the system into low resolution, was the ZGRASS just supposed to have its own graphic chip and local memory, and override through the video input?"

I want to clarify that the Z-GRASS on the add-under for the Astrocade would have been low-res only, but Z-GRASS on the UV-1 would have supported hi-res mode.  Of course, this UV-R1 computer in January 1983, cost $7,695 (!).  Here are two ads for the UV-1:

1) Datamax UV-1R Zgrass Graphics Computer Flyer

https://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/Zgrass_Graphics_Computer_Flyer/Datamax_UV-1R_Zgrass_Graphics_Computer.pdf

2)  Datamax UV-1R Zgrass Graphics System Flyer

https://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/zgrass/UV-1R_System_Flyer/Datamax_UV-1R_Zgrass_Graphics_System.pdf

There are a few examples of videos from 1980-1985 that were created using the Z-GRASS language on the UV-1.  My site has links to a few of them that are on YouTube, here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/astrocade_videos/Datamax_UV-1_Videos/Datamax_UV-1_Videos.html

There are some rare computers out there in the world.  The UV-1 must be among the rarest of them all, if any even still exist.

Adam
